Letter to the editor
Response to “Does ALR deficiency pave the way for NASH progression?”
Alok K. Verma, Chandrashekhar R. Gandhi
Department of Pediatrics, Cincinnati Children’s Hospital Medical Center, Cincinnati, 
Ohio
We appreciate the important points raised by Weiss et al. Our data indicate that the loss of 
21/23 kDa ALR, in mouse and human, renders the liver compromised to develop NASH(1). 
Administration of 21/23 kDa ALR to hepatocyte-specific ALR-knockout (ALR- H-KO) mice 
between 1 and 2 weeks postpartum mitigated steatohepatitis(2). The 15 kDa ALR is absent 
(Fig. 8)(1)(Ref. 71 in (3)) or expressed at very low level(4) in human liver, and absent in mouse 
liver(1,3,5). However, further investigation of ALR isoform(s) that can be of therapeutic 
interventions is important.
Hepatic ALR is down-regulated in steatosis regardless of its etiology in wild type (WT) 
mice, which do not develop inflammation or fibrosis(1,2,4,5). Only a subset of humans with 
NAFL develop NASH and some of these progress to cirrhosis, suggesting that inherent 
deficiency or anomaly in ALR could be an important predisposing factor. However, it will

be of interest to examine FOXA2 or NRF2 during NAFLD progression due to diet-induced or 
inherent ALR deficiency.
In the papers identified by Weiss et al(3), ALR is less stable (probably also less efficient) 
due to the rare mutation(s) in GFER gene in the affected patients. The mutations were 
associated with congenital cataract, and muscular hypotonia and developmental delay. 
Note that liver biopsy of only one patient was performed, which showed mitochondrial
Accepted Article

damage and fibrosis. Although studying the effect of high fat (HF) diet in mice with these 
mutation(s) in organ-specific manner is interesting, they are unlikely to be present in 
NASH, a global epidemic. Other mutations identified in GFER gene in general population(5) 
are being investigated.
Our conclusion that inherent ALR deficiency or anomaly could be critical in NASH 
progression to cirrhosis was based on (1) HF diet-induced excessive steatosis, 
inflammation and fibrosis in otherwise normal ALR-H-heterozygous mice, and augmented 
inflammation and cirrhosis in ALR-H-KO mice with pre-existing underlying pathology; and
(2) lower ALR levels in human NASH and NASH-cirrhosis(1,4,5). However, high ALR 
expression observed in some NASH-cirrhotic livers (Supporting Fig. 10; Supporting Table 
4)(1) indicates heterogeneity in human NASH. Patients expressing higher hepatic ALR had 
non-NASH cirrhosis[Ref. 71 in (3)], which may be attributed to etiological differences from 
NASH-cirrhosis.
